introduction: Fair warning. This is an embellished fictional dramatization that may or may not be based on true stories. The narrator is a guy named Charlie Hack. Any resemblance to me is mostly coincidental. Names, characters, companies and events are fictitious, or used fictitiously.
This preview jumps into the middle of the book. Part Three. C Things That Looked Like A Things.

Silicon Valley is very good at telling a story about A players. The people who look like they were always going to win. The companies that look like they were always going to work. The myth is a straight line: a garage, a genius, a ticker symbol. Most of the real work looks nothing like that. It looks like another ordinary Tuesday, doing the next right thing.
From the outside, a C thing can look like an A thing. Applause is loud. The real work is quieter. The book is about that gap: what people saw, and what was really going on.
A C player is not a failure. A C player is the person who was never the smartest in the room, and kept going anyway. There's always someone smarter, richer, wiser. Stay humble. Stay curious.

The Valley falls in love with products. Specific wins. Specific years. I got more out of building a platform: a foundation you can stand on, and build the next thing on, and the thing after that. You don't invent a career in one move. You stack building blocks. Habits. Fundamentals. The unglamorous layer nobody puts on a slide. That layer is what you actually stand on later.
It's all relative, how good you look from the outside. I just kept going. And I kept doing my best.

Then the work itself changed. I'm usually the most excited person in the room about AI. Which is funny, because I should be the saddest. AI came after the code writers first. In my view, AI now writes essentially all of the code. So gear your software engineering practices around that. That's what Software Engineering 101 and 201 are about, and the second half of this book: how to work now, and how companies should use AI.

The book begins with a green-screen dream. It ends by dreaming about AI. This part, in the middle, is the turn. It's free. It's open. And when version one is ready, if you were around for any of it, you get to tell your side. The story is still being written.

outline.title: Story arc and chapters
outline.note: This is a working outline. It will change as chapters are written, as interviews fill gaps, and as people contribute.
outline.throughline: A C player who kept going, dreamed in green screen, watched AI come for the coders first, and now shows you how to work.

halves.title: First half: The career arc
halves.summary: School days, then the jobs in career order, then the turn when AI came for the code writers.

chapters.title: Disclaimer
chapters.hook: An embellished fictional dramatization that may or may not be based on true stories. Names, characters, companies and events are fictitious or used fictitiously.

chapters.title: Introduction
chapters.hook: Top of the class, middle of the pack, a career of C companies. A C player is the person who was never the smartest in the room, and kept going anyway.

chapters.title: Prologue: Dreaming in Green
chapters.hook: Three students, one MIDI machine, the same Tron-like dream of logic gates during CS150 all-nighters. Real life bled into their dreams.

chapters.title: Top of the Class
chapters.hook: The kid who was used to being first.

chapters.title: No Curve
chapters.hook: "We were all stupid American kids." Cs and Ds on the first Math 1A midterm. No curve. It hit hard.

chapters.title: The A+ I Didn't Earn
chapters.hook: A music elective where he barely did anything, wrote a baroque music composer, and almost everyone got an A+.

chapters.title: The Weeder and the B-Minus
chapters.hook: Top of CS61B with an A+, then a B-minus in Algorithms. It's all relative, how smart you are.

chapters.title: The Lab Partner's Grade
chapters.hook: Shared project: the narrator got an A; his lab partner, who was brilliant, got an A-minus and was livid. He's not saying he was smarter. He just kept going.

chapters.title: Fundamentals Nobody Uses
chapters.hook: Bayview taught ideas, not languages: COOL, Lambda, B-trees, a compiler, digital circuits — principles that outlive tools.

chapters.title: Seventy Thousand at Ground Level
chapters.hook: Interned at Pixel Drift while still at Bayview, then took his first full-time job there at $70K out of college, $90K after year one. Pixel Drift was acquired by Spreewald Digital, a Berlin company.

chapters.title: Money Was Flowing
chapters.hook: The dot-com boom in San Francisco, "there at ground level."

chapters.title: Beer in Canoes
chapters.hook: Spreewald Digital trips: visiting East Berlin, and a company retreat drinking beer on canoes.

chapters.title: Three Million at Twenty-Five
chapters.hook: A $3M exit at 25. Which company that exit came from is still an open question.

chapters.title: Gulf Coast
chapters.hook: Years on the Gulf Coast at Bayou Ledger.

chapters.title: PRISM After Dark
chapters.hook: A night story from RentRiver.

chapters.title: Sold to WireHorse
chapters.hook: Co-founded RentRiver; acquired by WireHorse Global. The deal itself needs a story.

chapters.title: Untitled
chapters.hook: A later chapter back at Bayou Ledger, in a bigger role.

chapters.title: San Francisco After Dark
chapters.hook: A founder's apartment, nights out in the city, all-night coding sessions.

chapters.title: Before the IPO
chapters.hook: Co-founder and CTO of Swipewell, a card startup that went public after he left. What happened to the equity needs a story.

chapters.title: Options, Not Salary
chapters.hook: The money-years rule: stock options, not salary, are how people build real wealth. Which deal taught it needs a story.

chapters.title: The C Thing
chapters.hook: The one that looked like an A to everyone. What people saw, and what was really going on.

chapters.title: CTO, Again and Again
chapters.hook: LoanLark, LeaseLoop, Gumdrop.io, eSteward, HonestNest, in career order: the serial CTO. Each company needs a story.

chapters.title: The Smarter Guy in the Room
chapters.hook: There's always someone smarter, richer, wiser. Stay humble, stay curious. A specific moment needs a story.

chapters.title: Falling and Getting Up
chapters.hook: A failure, and getting back up. "I just kept going."

chapters.title: Untitled
chapters.hook: A reserved chapter, included only if Clark chooses to put it in the book.

sections.title: The turn: AI came for the coders first

chapters.title: The Saddest Man in the Room
chapters.hook: The most AI-excited person in the room should be the saddest: AI came for the code writers first. The specific day still needs a story.

chapters.title: Seventy, Eighty, Ninety, One Hundred
chapters.hook: A year ago people said 70, 80, 90 percent. Clark's view is that AI now writes 100% of the code. Public surveys still range widely; the book will present his view alongside those numbers.

chapters.title: I'd Never Built a Mobile App
chapters.hook: One shot to fix an app, and he had never built a mobile app — shipped with agents.

chapters.title: Changing My Tune
chapters.hook: He used to be a pragmatist on unit tests; once tests got cheap, he changed his mind and wanted more of them.

halves.title: Second half: This site, and where it goes
halves.summary: How to work now, drawn from the lessons on this site; then the OpenBook itself, how agents can use the site, the weekly improvement loop, and how companies should use AI.
halves.note: Each how-to chapter opens with a short story, then the rules. The site lessons are the primary text; the book version is rewritten for reading.

chapters.title: Show It, Don't Describe It
chapters.hook: Paste first; don't just describe the problem.

chapters.title: "Done" Is Not Proof
chapters.hook: A bot that says "done" is reporting a step, not your outcome.

chapters.title: What It Can Reach
chapters.hook: Know what an agent can actually reach, and put real locks in settings.

chapters.title: Teach It Once
chapters.hook: Memory is notes, not a mind. Skills, projects, handoffs.

chapters.title: The Second Message, and Other Everyday Moves
chapters.hook: Most people read the first answer and stop.

chapters.title: The Loop
chapters.hook: Plan, build, verify, and when to skip it. Rigor follows risk. Can open with the mobile-app story from chapter 21.

chapters.title: The Ladder
chapters.hook: AI coding is one more rung, from first principles up. Callback to the fundamentals chapter and the green-screen prologue.

chapters.title: Old Patterns at Agent Speed
chapters.hook: Pairing, TDD, and small ships still work; they just run faster.

chapters.title: Money and Data
chapters.hook: Treat AI usage carefully; never risk customer data.

chapters.title: From Loop to Enterprise Systems
chapters.hook: 101 is the loop; 201 builds whole systems AI-native: decompose them into a graph, run agents in parallel and integrate, govern where people decide, measure quality and observe, turn repeated work into skills, wire routines and pipelines, and let agents operate enterprise systems with permissions and audit, ending with a capstone that builds one feature end to end. Lesson 9 is still an outline; lesson 10 is the capstone.

chapters.title: The OpenBook
chapters.hook: A free book that works like open-source software: anyone can contribute a story or a correction from day one; credits are by GitHub handle; only Clark publishes. When version one is ready, a wider invitation goes out to people who recognize a story.

chapters.title: Built for Agents
chapters.hook: Every page has a Markdown twin and an AGENTS.md. The site index is llms.txt. Readers can search in the browser, send a cited prompt to their own AI, or connect through a public, read-only MCP endpoint, so an agent can use the site the way a person can.

chapters.title: A Site That Improves Itself
chapters.hook: A weekly routine looks at the site as a person, as an agent, and as the content owner, then files issues and opens staging pull requests. The first run has not happened yet.

chapters.title: How Companies Should Use AI
chapters.hook: From one engineer and an agent to a company running a fleet.

chapters.title: Epilogue: Dreaming in AI
chapters.hook: Years after the green screen, dreaming again, this time about AI.

chapters.title: The story is still being written
chapters.hook: The book stays open, like a living repo.

chapters.title: Appendix: The Rules
chapters.hook: Every rule from the how-to half, plus links to the site and llms.txt.
